newsitem.title: USA: Jesse Jackson joins Clinton's bully pulpit on race.
newsitem.headline: Jesse Jackson joins Clinton's bully pulpit on race.

text.p: Rev. Jesse Jackson, opening the annual convention of the civil rights group he heads, said Wednesday blacks need to participate in the national debate on race begun by President Clinton.

"The president has raised the race debate," Jackson told reporters at the start of his National Rainbow/PUSH Coalition's convention. "But so far, our scholars have not convened to examine the race question."
Jackson said the convention will focus on improving education and employment opportunities, expanding markets and planning for maximum policy impact.
Sessions will feature prominent black leaders as well as executives from large corporations such as the Big Three automakers and others.

"I'm convinced corporate America has been guilty of restraint of trade behind the barriers of race and sex," Jackson said. He has led several boycotts of corporations seeking greater opportunities for blacks.

"Times are tense, and many of our people are still locked out, dispossessed, marginalized. But we must never forget -- this is a different America that stands on the cusp of a new century than the apartheid America that W.E.B. DuBois viewed in 1900," Jackson said.
Jackson, who denied speculation he would use the convention to announce a third run for the presidency in 2000, said the 1998 mid-term elections were his focus for now.

On Aug. 28, the civil rights group will commemorate the anniversary of the 1964 march on Washington led by Martin Luther King Jr. by staging a march in California against the state's ban on preferences in university admissions.
He also spent much time on the issue of education. Last year, Jackson injected himself into the Oakland, California, school system's controversy over the use of "Ebonics" or black english.
He said his Chicago-based group, which has offices in Washington and in New York's financial district, would seek to "bring 2 million parents and children back to school."

He said clergymen would be called upon to have each church save 20 youths caught up in the juvenile justice system. He said parents and children would be urged to sign written pledges that would require students to turn off the television and study, and parents to meet their children's teachers and review report cards.
"No one is too busy to care for their child, or too poor," Jackson said.

Appearing with Jackson was Paul Vallas, the head of Chicago's public school system who has spearheaded a host of reforms that led to Jackson to call the city's schools "the flagship for the (national movement) to rejuvenate schools."
"What Rev. Jackson does ... he elevates those issues to a national stage," Vallas said.
